title: Knee injections in frail adults: questions worth asking (UK)

direct_answer: Steroid injections into the knee can give short-term relief for osteoarthritis pain when other treatments have not helped enough. NICE does not recommend hyaluronic acid injections for osteoarthritis. Exercise remains the core treatment. Ask about benefits, risks and how often injections can be repeated.

content:
Knee pain from osteoarthritis can limit walking and independence. Injections are one option, alongside other treatments.

This guide explains common types and questions to ask. It is educational information, not a diagnosis or personal treatment plan.

Steroid injections

NICE suggests considering steroid injections for short-term relief of osteoarthritis pain when other treatments have not been effective, to support exercise.

Other injections

NICE recommends against offering hyaluronic acid injections for osteoarthritis. Other treatments, such as platelet-rich plasma, are not routinely offered on the NHS.

Questions to ask

  • How long might the benefit last?
  • What are the risks, such as infection or raised blood sugar if I have diabetes?
  • How often can I have one?
  • What should I do afterwards?
  • How does this fit with my exercise plan?

Alongside injections

Exercise, weight management and pain relief remain important.

When to get help

  • Get urgent help from NHS 111 or your GP if the joint becomes hot, red, very swollen or painful, or you have a fever after an injection.

Never stop or change a prescribed medicine yourself. Ask your GP or pharmacist for a review.

Common questions

Are injections a cure?

No. They may reduce pain for a while.

Can I have an injection if I take blood thinners?

Tell your clinician about all your medicines.

Sources and further reading

  • NHS: Steroid injections
  • NICE NG226: Osteoarthritis in over 16s
  • NHS: Osteoarthritis treatment
